title: Betelgeuse Has a Partner After All
hook: A century of suspicion, finally imaged: astronomers have their clearest picture yet of the star hiding in Betelgeuse's glare — and it's heavier than anyone expected.
key_points: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant so large and so bright that anything orbiting close to it is drowned in its light.
Astronomers have now captured the clearest image yet of a long-suspected companion star, a search that ran for roughly a century.
The companion looks surprisingly massive, which changes what kind of object it can be and how it formed alongside Betelgeuse.
A close companion offers a natural explanation for Betelgeuse's long-puzzling swings in brightness.
It may also shape how Betelgeuse eventually explodes — supernovae in binaries can look quite different from solitary ones.
content_html: Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion, is one of the most-watched stars in the sky, and for about a century astronomers have suspected it isn't alone. The problem was always visibility: the supergiant is so vast and so luminous that a nearby companion sits buried in its glare. Astronomers now report their clearest image yet of that hidden partner — and it appears surprisingly massive.
extra_html: The find matters for two reasons. First, Betelgeuse's brightness has long wobbled in ways that stubbornly resist explanation — including the "Great Dimming" that briefly had people wondering whether it was about to explode. A close companion is exactly the kind of thing that can drive such variability. Second, having a partner can change how a massive star dies: mass exchange and orbital dynamics in a binary leave their mark on the resulting supernova. Reported by ScienceDaily on 27 August 2026; details and the imaging data are in the source.

related.hook: Stars are born in collapsing gas clouds, spend their lives fusing hydrogen into helium, then die in ways that depend entirely on how heavy they are.

related.hook: When a giant star dies, its core collapses and its outer layers blast away in a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy — leaving behind something extraordinary.

related.title: Magnetic Brakes for Newborn Stars
related.hook: Half the stars in the sky come in pairs, but making them is tricky. Simulations suggest magnetic fields act as a brake that lets two protostars spiral together.

related.title: A Supernova That Peeled Back a Star's Layers
related.hook: A rare supernova exposed material from one of the deepest layers of a dying star — a direct look inside the element factory hidden in massive stars.

flashcards.prompt: Why did it take about a century to image Betelgeuse's companion?
flashcards.back_html: Betelgeuse is an enormous, extremely bright red supergiant. Anything orbiting nearby is lost in its glare, so the companion had to be inferred long before it could be seen.

flashcards.prompt: Which long-standing Betelgeuse puzzle does a close companion help explain?

choices.text: Why it is redder than other supergiants
Why it emits no detectable gravitational waves

flashcards.explanation_html: Betelgeuse's brightness variability has puzzled observers for decades; a close orbiting companion gives that variability a natural mechanism.

flashcards.prompt: Beyond brightness, what else could the companion affect?
flashcards.back_html: Betelgeuse's eventual supernova. A star that explodes with a close companion can behave — and look — quite differently from one that dies alone.
